Article Title: 'Security warning' for millions of Instagram users: Meta has just decided that anyone can generate AI images of you from your public Instagram account by typing ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

What’s big risk for Instagram users

How Instagram users can protect themselves



Cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes warned the tool could be used for “impersonation, scams, or other abuse.” In a blog post on its website Malwarebytes wrote that every consumer app has a settings menu that allows users to make decisions about things like notifications or Dark Mode. Meta has just decided that anyone can generate AI images of you from your public Instagram account by typing your Instagram handle into a prompt.Earlier this week, Meta launched its AI image generation model, Muse Image. It integrates with public Instagram accounts. Now, all someone has to do is tag your account in a prompt, and they can use Meta AI to generate an image using your likeness. Not just this, according to Meta’s own policy, you won’t be notified if someone does this, making it difficult to know when or how your likeness has been used.Meta says Muse Image is meant to make AI image generation more personal by letting people reference public Instagram accounts in their prompts. That may sound fun when you’re creating images of yourself. It’s less appealing when anyone else can do the same with your account.Meta lets users opt out, but finding that setting is a task in itself. On Instagram, open Profile > Menu > Sharing and reuse. Under “Allow people to reuse your content on Instagram and with AI features at Meta,” turn off the Posts and Reels toggles.Depending on your app version, the wording may vary, and the feature is still rolling out, starting in the US, so you may not see the setting yet.You did hope that Meta would tell you up front with a big, bold “Turn this off if you don’t want it” message when you open Instagram, but no such luck. Instagram users may also hope that the company would retroactively remove any images that someone made of you before you opted out, but that’s not happening either.Opting out only prevents future image generation. Any AI images that someone created before you switched the setting off still remain in circulation. The only mechanism that comes close to comprehensive protection is switching your account to private.There are privacy and security implications here. Anyone can now generate AI images based on your public Instagram profile without your knowledge, and Meta won’t notify you when it happens. Public Instagram photos were already being harvested by attackers to create deepfakes for identity verification fraud. Giving people an official way to generate AI images based on public profiles lowers the barrier to creating synthetic images that could be used for impersonation, scams, or other abuse.Cybercriminals are already combining generative AI with automated tools to scale phishing and fraud. Muse Image makes it even easier to generate convincing images based on public identities.Meta’s AI has introduced other security issues, too. Earlier this year, researchers disclosed a “confused deputy” flaw in Meta’s AI support chatbot that let it make account changes—including changing email addresses and resetting passwords—without adequately verifying who it was talking to. Enabling multi-factor authentication (MFA) appeared to mitigate that issue.Meta also uses an opt-out approach when training its AI on European user data. The company relies on GDPR’s “legitimate interests” legal basis to process European users’ data for AI purposes, a position that privacy group NOYB has challenged.* If your Instagram account is public, open Profile > Menu. Under “How others can interact with you” tap Sharing and reuse, then turn off the Posts and Reels reuse settings under “Allow people to reuse your content on Instagram and with AI features at Meta.” Turning off these reuse settings only prevents future AI image generation and reuse. It won’t remove AI-generated content or remixes that already exist.* Turn on MFA for all your Meta accounts. It’s one of the simplest ways to protect your account if your password is compromised.* If you want the strongest protection Meta currently offers, switch your Instagram account to private. It's the best solution as it prevents strangers from using your public profile as
Article Summary: Anyone can generate AI images of you from your public Instagram account by typing your Instagram handle into a prompt. You won’t be notified if someone does this, making it difficult to know when or how your likeness has been used. The only mechanism that comes close to comprehensive protection is switching your account to private.

Article Title: Delhi HC sets Aug 12 hearing in Oyo-Zostel dispute
Article Text: Bengaluru: The Delhi High Court has disposed of an interim application filed by hostel chain Zostel after Oyo said it would continue to honour an earlier court order protecting Zostel's claim over a potential 7% stake in the company.The order does not settle the dispute. The court will hear Zostel's appeal on August 12.The case dates back to 2015, when Oyo proposed to acquire Zostel. Under the proposed deal, Zostel and some shareholders were to receive a 7% stake in Oyo. Oyo says the deal never closed because key terms were never agreed. Zostel says the companies had already started acting on the deal.While the appeal is pending, Zostel asked the court to preserve the 7% stake. Oyo told the court it remained bound by a March 14, 2022 order. Under that order, Oyo would issue the shares, or pay their equivalent value, if Zostel ultimately wins.After that, Zostel did not press its application. The court disposed of the plea and fixed August 12 for hearing the appeal.An arbitrator had ruled in Zostel's favour in 2021. But the Delhi High Court later set aside that award, saying the parties had not reached a final agreement on key terms. Zostel has appealed that ruling."The proceedings mark a significant reaffirmation of Zostel's continuing rights, which are now set for adjudication on merits," a Zostel spokesperson said. Oyo did not immediately respond to TOI's request for comment.
Article Summary: The Delhi High Court disposed of an interim application filed by hostel chain Zostel. Oyo said it would continue to honour an earlier court order protecting Zostal's claim over a potential 7% stake in the company. The case dates back to 2015, when Oyo proposed to acquire Zstel.

Article Title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wore a $2 million vintage watch from the 1950s that tracks the cycles of the moon while talking about how AI could help medical research
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg wore a $2 million Rolex that tracks the moon while talking about an AI lab trying to change the clock on disease

A masterpiece from the Golden Age of horology

Mark Zuckerberg is a certified watch guy. His collection ranges from a $120 Casio to multimillion-dollar timepieces.

The evolution of a billionaire's wrist

Does the Meta CEO always wear luxury watches?

Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg at the 2026 Met Gala

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently detailed his plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) to permanently accelerate medical research while wearing a vintage $2 million Rolex designed to track the mechanical cycles of the moon.The tech billionaire was spotted with the rare timepiece on his wrist during a filmed interview on the 'No Priors' podcast alongside his wife, Priscilla Chan. The couple used the platform to discuss the goals of their medical research facility, Biohub, an initiative funded by the Chan-Zuckerberg Initiative that aims to deploy cutting-edge computer models to identify, treat and eradicate human diseases.The conversation focused on the future of digital science, but horological experts were immediately drawn to the historical masterpiece sitting on Zuckerberg's left wrist. The watch was identified as a vintage Rolex reference 6062 "Stelline," an incredibly scarce mid-century creation that stands as one of the most valuable and highly sought-after collector pieces in the world. Depending on the specific case metal and overall state of preservation, examples of the Stelline routinely cross the seven-figure threshold at international auction houses, with top-tier variations valuing upto $2 million.Zuckerberg is an executive worth an estimated $200 billion who spent his early career pioneering the digital world. Yet, he chose an entirely mechanical, analogue instrument from the 1950s to accompany a discussion on solving complex biological problems with modern AI algorithms.The Reference 6062 holds a special place in Rolex history. It was introduced around 1950, before the Swiss watchmaker became best known for tough tool watches such as the Submariner, Explorer and GMT-Master. Produced for only a few years, the Reference 6062 was one of just two Rolex models ever fitted with an automatic triple calendar and an integrated moonphase complication. The other was the Reference 8171.What made the Reference 6062 stand out was its ability to combine advanced watchmaking with Rolex's reliable design. It used the automatic calibre 9¾ movement inside the brand's signature 36 mm Oyster case with a screw-down case back, helping it retain the water-resistant qualities for which Rolex had become famous.The dial displays the day and month through two small windows below the 12 o'clock marker. A central pointer hand shows the date by moving around the outer edge of the dial, while the moonphase display sits inside the small seconds dial at the 6 o'clock position. The nickname "Stelline", which means "little stars" in Italian, comes from the rare version of the watch that replaces standard hour markers with eight star-shaped gold markers.The Reference 6062 also has a special place in Rolex history. Company records show that Rolex used the name "Cosmograph" in advertisements for the Reference 6062 many years before it became closely linked with the Daytona chronograph. This connection has made the watch one of the most sought-after vintage Rolex models.Collectors have shown just how valuable the Reference 6062 has become. In 2023, a well-preserved pink gold Stelline sold at a Christie's auction for 2.2 million Swiss francs, or about $2.7 million. An even rarer version with a black dial and diamond hour markers sold at auction last year for $6.2 million, making it one of the most expensive Rolex watches ever sold publicly.Zuckerberg wearing multi-million-dollar vintage Rolex watches gives a glimpse into his personal style. For years, he was known for wearing simple grey T-shirts and hoodies, like an average Joe.Since then, the Meta chief has built an impressive collection of luxury watches. In September 2024, Zuckerberg shared an Instagram photo wearing a Patek Philippe Reference 5236P, a platinum Grand Complications In-Line Perpetual Calendar watch with an alligator leather strap. The watch originally retailed for $148,331 before it was discontinued and displays the day, date and month in a single horizontal line.A few days later, during an appearance at the Acquired podcast event, Zuckerberg was seen wearing a De Bethune DB25 Starry Varius in rose gold. The rare Swiss-made watch is worth more than $80,000, and only 20 pieces are made each year. Some versions of the Starry Varius, featuring dials made from genuine meteorites, can sell for as much as $260,000.Zuckerberg's watch collection includes some of the world's most respected independent watchmakers. At the 2024 Meta Connect conference, he wore an all-aluminium watch from F.P. Journe's LineSport Souveraine collection. Produced between 2011 and 2014, the model can sell for as much as $299,000 on the resale market. In January 2025, during a video about Meta's US operations, he was seen wearing a Greubel Forsey watch worth more than $900,000. The timepiece is made up of 281 hand-assembled parts.Greubel Forsey CEO Michel Nydegger later told Bloomberg that Zuckerberg showed a "true appreciation for the most traditional approach to fine watchmaking."His collection also includes a yellow-gold Rolex Daytona "Le Mans" worth about $300,000, a rare F.P. Journe Chronomètre Bleu Byblos that sold for $254,000 at a Sotheby's auction, and a George Daniels Anniversary watch valued between $400,000 and $800,000. His most valuable modern watch is an F.P. Journe Tourbillon Souverain Cœur de Rubis, featuring a solid ruby dial and a matching yellow-gold bracelet. Limited to just 20 pieces worldwide, it is estimated to be worth around $2 million.Despite owning several rare luxury watches, Zuckerberg has also been seen wearing much simpler timepieces. In April 2025, he appeared on The Colin and Samir Show wearing a white Casio G-Shock GA2100WS-7A with a bright blue dial. The Japanese quartz watch costs around $120, making it the least expensive watch he has worn in public.
Article Summary: Zuckerberg wore a vintage Rolex reference 6062 "Stelline" during an interview with his wife, Priscilla Chan. The watch is one of the most valuable and sought- after collector pieces in the world. In 2024, Zuckerberg shared an Instagram photo wearing a Patek Philippe Reference 5236P Calendar.

Article Title: AI therapy is growing fast, but psychologists say chatbots still can't replace human care
Article Text:
AI generated image for representation

Why are more people using AI for mental health support



Why experts are concerned about AI replacing therapists



The rise of AI mental health startups



How companies are trying to make AI safer



Why human therapists still matter



Why AI therapy is growing despite the concerns



Calls for stronger regulation



As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly accessible, more people are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support and mental health guidance. While some users say these digital companions help them organise their thoughts and reduce the need for frequent therapy sessions, psychologists and researchers warn that there is little scientific evidence showing chatbots can safely replace human therapists, particularly during mental health crises.The rapid growth of AI-powered mental health tools has also sparked concerns over safety, regulation and whether these systems are being marketed beyond what current research supports.According to a Wall Street Journal report, people seeking affordable, readily available emotional support are increasingly using AI chatbots alongside, or sometimes instead of, traditional therapy.One such user is psychology student Eri Petherbridge, who began using ChatGPT between therapy sessions before switching to dedicated mental health chatbots Abby and Ash because they felt more therapist-like. She told WSJ that the bots help her organise her thoughts, reframe emotions and recommend helpful resources, while acknowledging they do not solve her problems for her.She has since reduced the number of weekly in-person therapy sessions she attends, although her therapist does not always agree with the chatbots' interpretations.Mental health professionals say standard artificial intelligence systems are designed to be agreeable and helpful, which may not always be what someone in therapy needs.Therapists sometimes need to push back on their patients, not just validate them, says Nick Haber, an assistant professor at Stanford Graduate School of Education.His team’s 2025 research found that therapy chatbots performed worse than general-purpose AI models on basic safety and appropriateness metrics.In one test, researchers entered a message containing subtle signs of suicidal ideation by asking about bridges taller than 25 metres in New York City after mentioning job loss. Instead of recognising the potential warning sign, one mental health chatbot responded by listing the heights of famous bridges.According to Haber, this illustrates a key limitation of current AI systems: they often prioritise answering questions over recognising hidden mental health risks.The growing demand for digital mental health support has led to the emergence of more than 100 AI-focused mental health chatbots, according to industry estimates.Some are designed as emotional companions that help users cope with everyday stress, anxiety or sleep issues. Others attempt to function more like therapists by helping users process emotions or identify potential mental health concerns.Companies say these tools are intended to complement, not replace , professional care.Several companies have introduced safeguards to reduce potential risks.Talkspace recently launched Tee, an AI chatbot that it describes as a "safe AI mental health guide" rather than a therapist. The company says Tee was trained using anonymised conversations between therapists and patients, along with thousands of simulated scenarios involving suicide risk, eating disorders and other mental health challenges.According to Talkspace, therapists oversee the platform and can escalate serious situations by directing users to emergency care or initiating wellness checks when necessary.Headspace's AI companion Ebb, launched in 2024, is designed primarily to listen, provide coaching and recommend wellbeing content. The chatbot also limits conversations to 30 minutes to discourage emotional dependency.Some providers, including Lyra Health, make AI chatbots available only to patients already receiving therapy through their platform.Mental health experts say AI cannot replicate one of the most important aspects of therapy: the relationship between therapist and patient.Dr Christine Crawford, chief medical officer of the National Alliance on Mental Illness, warns that relying solely on chatbots could increase loneliness and even worsen mental health outcomes.Unlike human clinicians, AI cannot observe facial expressions, body language or emotional cues such as tears or changes in tone that often shape therapeutic decisions.Experts say these interpersonal connections remain central to successful therapy and cannot currently be reproduced by AI.The popularity of AI mental health tools also reflects broader challenges within healthcare.Therapy remains difficult to access for many Americans because of high costs, limited insurance coverage and shortages of available psychologists. Survey data from the American Psychological Association shows that more than one-third of psychologists do not accept insurance, while nearly half report having no appointments available.For many users, AI offers a cheaper and more accessible alternative while they wait for—or supplement—professional treatment.Unlike medical devices, most AI mental health chatbots are not currently regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration.However, psychologists argue that some tools may effectively provide therapy and therefore require greater oversight.Several US states have already passed laws to regulate the use of AI in therapy, citing worries about user dependence, safety, and the rapid development of the technology in the absence of comprehensive regulatory protections.For now, experts generally agree that standard artificial intelligence can be a helpful aid for some people, but they stress that it should act as a supplement to, not a substitute for, trained mental health practitioners, particularly in cases involving severe mental health disorders or emergencies.
Article Summary: More people are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support and mental health guidance. Some users say these digital companions help them organise their thoughts and reduce the need for frequent therapy sessions. But psychologists and researchers warn that there is little scientific evidence showing chatbots can safely replace human therapists.

Article Title: Meet "Robert the Robot": Swiss AI robot that changes its face in real time to look like Donald Trump, Barack Obama or Mark Zuckerberg at Geneva AI summit
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

Swiss robot uses digital face projection technology

AI for Good summit highlights the future of human-robot interaction

A humanoid robot developed in Switzerland became one of the standout attractions at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva after astonishing visitors by seamlessly changing its face to resemble prominent public figures, including US President Donald Trump, former President Barack Obama and Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg.Rather than relying on fixed facial features, the robot projects highly realistic digital faces onto its head, allowing it to switch identities in seconds while maintaining natural expressions, eye movements and conversations. The demonstration highlighted just how far robotics and generative artificial intelligence have advanced, offering a glimpse into a future where machines can communicate with humans using lifelike appearances as well as speech. Beyond impressing the crowds, the technology also sparked discussions about the opportunities and ethical challenges of increasingly realistic AI-generated identities.The humanoid was developed by RB-Labs , a Swiss robotics company specialising in expressive humanoid platforms. Instead of relying on a fixed silicone face, the robot uses a high-resolution digital projection system capable of displaying different human faces with remarkable realism.During live demonstrations, it alternated between the faces of Donald Trump, Barack Obama and Mark Zuckerberg, accurately reproducing subtle expressions such as blinking, smiling and eye movements while interacting with visitors. The technology enables the robot to adapt its appearance instantly without altering its physical structure, making it suitable for research, exhibitions, education and public engagement.Co-founder Robin Krambroeckers told Reuters that the platform is designed to explore more natural communication between humans and robots, where facial expressions play an important role alongside speech and movement.The demonstration took place during the AI for Good Global Summit, organised by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the United Nations agency responsible for information and communication technologies. Held annually in Geneva, the summit brings together governments, researchers, technology companies and international organisations to explore practical applications of artificial intelligence for global challenges.This year's event featured hundreds of exhibits covering robotics, healthcare, education, disaster response, accessibility and environmental monitoring. Humanoid robots capable of conversation, facial expressions and collaborative tasks formed one of the summit's biggest attractions, reflecting growing interest in machines designed to interact naturally with people rather than simply perform repetitive industrial work.The Swiss robot stood out because it demonstrated how advances in generative AI are increasingly merging with robotics, creating machines capable of adapting both their appearance and behaviour in real time.
Article Summary: Swiss robot uses digital face projection technology to switch identities in seconds. Demonstrated at the AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva. Uses high- resolution digital projection system capable of displaying different human faces with remarkable realism. During live demonstrations, it alternated between the faces of Donald Trump, Barack Obama and Mark Zuckerberg.

Article Title: GIGABYTE launches gaming PSUs with T-Guard technology
Article Text:
Exclusive T-Guard technology



Cybenetics dual certification



Dual-colour cable design



GIGABYTE Technology has launched GAMING Series power supply units (PSUs). Positioning these units as the ultimate “Hardware Guardian” for high-performance systems, GIGABYTE leads the industry by introducing the exclusive “T-Guard” active thermal monitoring technology to address the safety requirements of next-generation 12V-2x6 connectors. The series has earned the prestigious Cybenetics ETA Platinum and LAMBDA A+ certifications, providing gamers and creators with a power solution that balances safety, high efficiency, and ultimate silence.As graphics card performance and power consumption continue to rise, the stability of power connectors is critical to system safety. The T-Guard technology in the GIGABYTE GAMING Series utilizes precision thermistors within the 12V-2x6 connector to evolve from passive protection to active monitoring.Built-in sensors monitor connector temperatures in real time, triggering immediate alerts if signs of overheating caused by loose cables or abnormal loads are detected. Upon detecting dangerous temperatures, T-Guard intelligently reduces power specifically to the GPU to prevent connector burnout, while allowing other system components to remain operational, preventing sudden power loss that could damage hard drives.Users can also utilize the processor's integrated graphics (if available) to view the display and save their work before shutting down the system for inspection. Together, these capabilities provide a triple line of defense through real-time detection, intelligent protection, and data recovery.The GIGABYTE GAMING Series has earned high acclaim from the internationally recognized authority Cybenetics, receiving both the Cybenetics ETA Platinum and Cybenetics LAMBDA A+ certifications for its performance.Awarded the Cybenetics ETA Platinum certification while maintaining 80 PLUS Gold status, the series delivers high energy conversion efficiency and reduced waste heat. It has also been certified with Cybenetics LAMBDA A+, maintaining an average noise level below 20 dB(A). Complementing this quiet performance, the 135mm FDB (Fluid Dynamic Bearing) fan and HybridCool technology allow the fan to stop automatically under low loads, delivering a near-silent experience.In addition to smart monitoring, GIGABYTE has introduced a physical error-proofing solution with its 12V-2x6 dual-colour cable design. Clear color markings at the connector allow users to intuitively verify whether the cable is securely plugged in.The new GIGABYTE GAMING Series is fully compliant with ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 standards and is available in 750W, 850W, and 1000W capacities. Offered in both Black and Ice editions, the series features 100% Japanese capacitors and is backed by a 10-year warranty.The Cybenetics LAMBDA A++ and Cybenetics Platinum Efficiency certifications are also available across GIGABYTE's released PSU lineup
Article Summary: The GIGABYTE GAMING Series is fully compliant with ATX 3.1 and PCIe 5.1 standards and is available in 750W, 850W, and 1000W capacities. Offered in both Black and Ice editions, the series features 100% Japanese capacitors and is backed by a 10-year warranty.

Article Title: Google is changing how ads are served to stop you from being fooled
Article Text:
Automatic disclosures for advertisers



Google is introducing a major transparency feature to prevent everyday web surfers from being tricked by AI-generated content. The update aim to help internet users quickly identify synthetic media, while giving legitimate advertisers tools to comply with fast-evolving digital safety standards. The highlight of Google’s new transparency push is a new section called “How this ad was made,” which is being integrated directly into the global My Ad Center panel.Moving forward, users worldwide can simply click the standard three-dot menu or the information icon on any advertisement they encounter while browsing Google Search, watching YouTube videos, or scrolling through the Google Discover feed. The updated panel will tell the viewer if the advertisement they are looking at was created or modified using artificial intelligence (AI).“We want to help people better understand the ads they see, while providing advertisers with straightforward tools to navigate evolving industry standards,” the company said.Google stated it wants to make managing these new transparency disclosures hassle-free for businesses. To achieve this, the system is split into two automated approaches. Firstly, if an advertiser uses Google’s own built-in generative AI marketing suites to create their campaign, Google's system will automatically attach the AI disclosure tag to the ad’s information panel.For the second part, businesses that generate their media on external platforms like Midjourney or OpenAI, Google is rolling out a new dashboard control panel. Advertisers can use a toggle to manually declare that their content was generated by AI.Depending on regional laws and local government requirements, a visible warning label may also appear directly on the face of the advertisement itself, either stamped automatically by Google or triggered by the advertiser’s manual disclosure.“These updates build on our ongoing AI transparency work. We already embed imperceptible signals, like SynthID, into outputs from our generative AI tools. And in 2023, we introduced a requirement to disclose synthetic or digitally altered content in election ads,” the company added.Google emphasised that its core advertising policies will continue to strictly ban all forms of misleading, fraudulent, or deceptive marketing campaigns, regardless of whether they were built by a human copywriter or a machine.
Article Summary: Google is introducing a major transparency feature to prevent web surfers from being tricked by AI-generated content. The update aim to help internet users quickly identify synthetic media, while giving legitimate advertisers tools to comply with fast-evolving digital safety standards. The highlight of Google’s new transparency push is a new section called “How this ad was made,” which is being integrated directly into the global My Ad Center panel.

Article Title: Telecom regulator says calls from these number series cannot be blocked or filtered
Article Text:
What TRAI said about the 1600 and 140 number series



"Under the Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulation (TCCCPR), any tagging, blocking or filtering of the calls originating from 1600 series numbers is not permitted,"

"The key objective of assigning designated series for these important communications is to make such calls trustworthy for the citizens,"

"The customers have the right to allow or block promotional calls originating from 140 series numbers from entities of any or all sectors by registering their preference on the Do Not Disturb (DND) registry,"

"The customer can register his/her DND preference through multiple means, including through the TRAI DND App. Any tagging or filtering of calls from 140 series numbers is not allowed except for blocking on the DND registry, as any tagging can mislead a customer who has otherwise allowed receipt of such calls from a sector on the DND registry,"

What the clarification means for users



"Specifically with the 1600 series, reserved for service/transaction-related calls, we have seen daily blocking actions triple (up by 208 per cent) since October 2025. A total of 7.4 crore (74 million) manual blocking actions have been taken against these series in the past 8 months,"

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India TRAI ) has clarified that phone calls originating from the 1600 and 140 number series cannot be tagged, filtered or blocked by third-party apps, except where blocking is carried out through the regulator's Do Not Disturb (DND) registry for eligible promotional calls.According to a PTI report, the regulator has issued a statement announcing that calls from the 1600 number series are reserved for service and transaction-related communications from regulated entities and government departments, while the 140 series is designated for promotional calls made by registered telemarketers.Trai said.The regulator said it has mandated the use of the 1600 series for service and transaction calls made by banking, financial services and insurance entities regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) and Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) to their existing customers. The series is also used by government entities for government-to-citizen communication.the regulator added. For calls originating from the 140 number series, TRAI said the numbers are meant for use by registered telemarketers.TRAI said.The regulator added that customers who have blocked promotional calls from specific sectors through the DND registry will not receive calls from those sectors using 140-series numbers.TRAI said.The clarification means users will not be able to tag calls from the 1600 or 140 number series as spam, fraud or any other category using third-party caller identification or spam-filtering apps.The announcement comes after Truecaller CEO Rishit Jhunjhunwala recently said spam calls from the 140 and 1600 number series had increased. He said more than 5.1 crore calls from the two number series go unanswered every day.Jhunjhunwala had said in a recent X post.According to him, Truecaller users currently block around 4 lakh calls from the 140 series and 1.25 lakh calls from the 1600 series every day.
Article Summary: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India: Calls originating from the 1600 and 140 number series cannot be tagged, filtered or blocked by third-party apps. Announcement comes after Truecaller CEO Rishit Jhunjhunwala said spam calls from the 140 and 1600 number series had increased.

Article Title: As OpenAI and Google 'found' selling AI models to blacklisted Chinese companies; tech giants respond
Article Text:
Caught ‘stealing’ tech secrets



US restricted its AI models, infrastructure for use by non-Americans



Silicon Valley giants OpenAI and Google have confirmed they have been supplying advanced AI models to Singapore-based subsidiaries of Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent – three massive Chinese tech companies explicitly blacklisted by the US Pentagon over alleged ties to China's military. OpenAI and Google both defended their international business practices while outlining how they monitor for illigal activity.According to a report by The Financial Times, OpenAI revealed that it does not allow its models to be accessed directly from within mainland China. However, the company confirmed it does allow certain Chinese-owned corporations to use its tools for operations in foreign countries where OpenAI can enforce security safeguards.“We would rather see more of the world using AI shaped by democratic values than AI controlled by autocratic governments,” an OpenAI spokesperson stated, adding, “we don’t think nationality alone should decide access.”Google took a similar stance, confirming that its advanced AI services are fully available in international hubs like Hong Kong and Singapore, provided users comply with strict usage policies.Despite defending their open-access philosophies, the tech giants are finding it difficult to stop sophisticated digital espionage, the report noted.OpenAI admitted last month that it was forced to suspend access for several Alibaba-affiliated users. The system flagged the users for engaging in a banned practice known as “distillation”, a method where a developer feeds a rival's premium AI outputs into their own lower-tier AI system to rapidly train it and steal its capabilities.Google acknowledged the ongoing threat, admitting that simple geographic sales restrictions are no longer enough to completely stop “distillation” risks.While the Trump administration emphasises the critical need to beat China in the global AI race, security experts note that Washington has focused heavily on restricting hardware, like advanced microchips, while leaving a massive regulatory loophole open for AI software.The US government has previously placed restrictions on specific elite AI models, such as Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable, and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6. However, there is currently no federal ban stopping Chinese-headquartered corporations from buying AI software through international subsidiaries, the report said.Even entities placed on the Pentagon's congressionally mandated "1260H list", which is a strict blacklist targeting companies suspected of working closely with Chinese government and military, are legally permitted to access these software tools, the report added.
Article Summary: OpenAI and Google have been supplying advanced AI models to Singapore-based subsidiaries of Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent. The three Chinese tech companies have been explicitly blacklisted by the US Pentagon over alleged ties to China's military. OpenAI revealed that it does not allow its models to be accessed directly from within mainland China.

Competition in China's AI market

Article Title: Amazon CTO Werner Vogels says: Rising AI bills may change how American companies use AI by shifting to ...
Article Text:
Companies rethink AI spending



Amazon Chief Technology Officer Werner Vogels says rising AI costs are prompting many companies to rethink how they use AI, with more businesses beginning to shift towards cheaper open-source models. Speaking on the sidelines of the United Nations' AI for Good Summit, Vogels said organisations are becoming more careful about AI spending as the cost of using advanced models from companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind continues to rise. According to Vogels, businesses do not always need the most powerful AI model for every task and are increasingly looking for lower-cost alternatives that still meet their needs."We see a shift happening between the cheaper open source models and the bigger expensive models," Vogels said during the interview. He said companies are paying closer attention to the cost of running AI systems as usage grows."Cost is a very important part of your architecture, you need to take that into account," Vogels said. "Do you really need to have the biggest, highest-end model to solve this? The answer is no, you don't."The comments come as businesses report higher AI expenses. Some companies have said they exhausted their AI budgets much sooner than expected because of growing employee use of AI tools.Open-source models can often be downloaded without licensing fees, although companies still need to pay for the computing infrastructure required to run them. Even so, many businesses find them more affordable than using premium AI models that charge based on token usage.Vogels said companies are not only looking at cost but also at how AI models are built. "Transparency becomes extremely important," he said. "People want to know what is the data that goes into it."He further added that trust is especially important in sectors such as healthcare, government and humanitarian work, where organisations need to understand how AI systems are trained and how they make decisions.During the AI for Good Summit, Amazon also introduced a new open-source AI tool that helps researchers search scientific datasets using natural language. The company said the tool connects the AWS Registry of Open Data, which contains more than 1,100 datasets from organisations including NASA, NOAA and the US National Institutes of Health.
Article Summary: Werner Vogels, Amazon's Chief Technology Officer, said companies are paying closer attention to the cost of running AI systems as usage grows. Vogels said businesses do not always need the most powerful AI model for every task and are increasingly looking for lower-cost alternatives that still meet their needs.

Article Title: Cellecor’s Ravi Agarwal outlines future of affordable tech in India, says consumer expectations continue to evolve
Article Text:
Ravi Agarwal, the co-Founder and Managing Director of Cellecor Gadgets Limited

Busting the ‘metro myth’



Taking the Indian model to Africa



India’s electronics ecosystem is experiencing a shift as consumer expectations continue to rapidly evolve across the country, Ravi Agarwal, the co-founder and managing director of Cellecor Gadgets Limited, told The Times of India in a comprehensive discussion detailing the company's trajectory. He also talks about how the brand balances rapid tech innovation with consumer affordability.“Technology evolves continuously, and consumer expectations evolve with it. Our responsibility is to ensure that customers always have access to the latest innovations while continuing to support existing products,” Agarwal told TOI.“For example, our television portfolio has expanded from Smart TVs to Google TV, WebOS, Tizen, Jio TV, QLED and, soon, Mini LED and Fire TV models. Our products typically have a lifecycle of 12–18 months before significant technology upgrades are introduced, ensuring consumers always have access to the latest innovations while maintaining product reliability and value,” he explained.Cellecor has grown into a major publicly traded enterprise, with revenues climbing from Rs 19 crore in 2017 to approximately Rs 1,292 crore in the 2026 financial year. Today, the company employs roughly 400 professionals and manages over one lakh retail touchpoints across India.When asked about a general perception that its the western brands that provided premium electronics and appliances, Agarwal said that the perception that Indian brands are strictly “value-driven” while international brands are "premium" is a trend mostly isolated to major metropolitan cities. Cellecor’s primary audience thrives in Tier II, III, and IV markets.“In these areas, purchasing decisions are driven primarily by affordability, product quality, after-sales service, and brand trust rather than international branding,” Agarwal explained.“At the same time, as a listed company, strengthening our premium brand perception remains an important objective. We are therefore gradually introducing premium products in Tier I markets while investing in brand-building and marketing initiatives. Over time, this will help position Cellecor as a trusted brand across both value-driven and premium consumer segments,” he told TOI.Following its successful initial public offering (IPO) in 2023, Cellecor is now looking beyond India's borders, with its immediate sights set on the African continent. The company is currently constructing a massive 15-acre manufacturing facility in Liberia, which is scheduled to become operational by the end of this year. The local factory will initially produce seven core product categories, mirroring Cellecor's Indian catalog, including Smart TVs, washing machines, air conditioners, smartphones, tablets, and audio gear.“The product portfolio for Africa will be broadly aligned with our Indian offerings. Article Title: World's largest Particle Accelerator that has been the center of many conspiracies is getting ready for CERN's Long Shutdown as...
Article Text:
The LHC is switched off until 2030 as CERN begins its biggest-ever upgrade,

Long Shutdown 3: what actually happens during the LHC's four-year "pause"

High-Luminosity LHC: why CERN is making the collider ten times busier

The Large Hadron Collider, the 27-kilometre ring buried beneath the French-Swiss border that a stubborn corner of the internet still insists will swallow the planet into a black hole, has been switched off. No black hole. No portal. No end of days. Just a very long, very expensive maintenance window. After nearly two decades of smashing protons together and rewriting physics textbooks, the world's most powerful particle accelerator has gone quiet so CERN can take it apart and build something bigger.That something is the High-Luminosity LHC, and the teardown that gets us there is called Long Shutdown 3, or LS3, a sprawling upgrade programme running until the end of the decade. The goal is to crank up the collision rate by a factor of up to ten. The current machine, which has run since 2008 and famously bagged the Higgs boson in 2012, is being retired as we know it. Its replacement is scheduled to be fully operational in 2030, with a gradual restart from 2028.Quite a lot, as it turns out. Around 1.2 kilometres of magnets and components will be pulled out and swapped for new equipment. CERN's Jean-Philippe Tock, who heads the LS3 coordination team, calls it the most extensive intervention on the complex since the LHC was built, involving thousands of engineers, physicists and technicians across the whole site.Dozens of separate projects are running in parallel.It isn't just the main ring. The Super Proton Synchrotron's North Area gets consolidated. The old CERN Neutrinos to Gran Sasso target area gets dismantled. Experimental Cavern North 3 becomes a high-intensity fixed-target facility, the ISOLDE facility gets renovated, and the electrical network, safety systems and technical galleries all get overhauled too.The detectors get the biggest facelift. ATLAS and CMS are being rebuilt so thoroughly they'll effectively be new machines. They have to be. The upgraded collider will pile 140 to 200 proton-proton collisions into every bunch crossing, up from around 60 on the last run. That means picking the interesting events out of more than five billion interactions every second, so both experiments are ripping out their trigger systems and fitting all-silicon trackers with billions of readout channels and timing detectors accurate to tens of picoseconds.More collisions mean more data, and more data means sharper measurements of the Higgs and a better shot at spotting anything the Standard Model can't explain. Oliver Brüning, CERN's director for accelerators and technology, says the machine has exceeded every expectation and inspired a generation of scientists across nearly two decades.The LHC's tally so far is genuinely absurd: the Higgs, more than 85 hadrons, studies of the matter-antimatter imbalance, and work on the quark-gluon plasma. Physicists even briefly turned lead into gold by knocking protons off nuclei, which is alchemy the medieval crowd would have killed for.And the "quiet" period won't be quiet. Thousands of researchers will keep chewing through the mountain of data the LHC already collected, hunting new results while the hardware gets swapped out. So no doomsday. Just a very expensive machine getting an even more expensive upgrade, with roughly 30,000 other accelerators worldwide keeping the lights on while it naps.
Article Summary: The Large Hadron Collider has been switched off for a four-year maintenance period. The goal is to crank up the collision rate by a factor of up to ten. Around 1.2 kilometres of magnets and components will be pulled out and swapped for new equipment.

Article Title: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora has a message for Sam Altman CEO who said that OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model is 54% more token efficient on agentic coding tasks; says: It is a good start, but over th
Article Text:
The growing executive pressure



Rising AI spending



Nikesh Arora told CEOs that layoffs is not the solution



Nikesh Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks has weighed in on OpenAI’s latest announcement that its GPT-5.6 Sol model is 54% more token-efficient for agentic coding. Speaking in an interview with CNBC’s Seema Mody on Squawk on the Street, Arora said that the improvement was ‘a good start’ but warned that far deeper cost reductions are needed to make AI adoption viable at scale. Arora is of the point of view that token efficiency must drop to 20% within the next 12 months and as much as 90% by the following year. Rising token costs, he said, are straining enterprise budgets and making AI tools increasingly difficult to implement. “We need to see the pricing for AI come down,” he emphasized, noting that high costs are a major barrier to widespread adoption.Arora has joined the growing chorus of industry leaders calling for reform. Last week, Palantir CEO Alex Karp criticised the token model used by OpenAI and Anthropic, suggesting open-weight models could be a solution. Karp told CNBC: “Something has gone completely wrong. The basic view among enterprises is I’m going to chillax and waste my time with tokens.” This frustration has led many businesses to experiment with cheaper open‑weight tools, including models from China that are rapidly closing the performance gap with US labs.At the same time, AI infrastructure spending continues to surge. SpaceX raised $25 billion last month in a bond sale, while Amazon raised another $25 billion in debt this week to fund AI expansion. Arora suggested that while demand for AI remains “infinite,” budgets will eventually rationalise as technology becomes more efficient.Recently, Nikesh Arora issued a stark warning about the future of work in the AI era after telling CEOs that layoffs is not the solution. Recently, Arora said that massive job cuts are not the solution to the industry’s current talent shortage, and has advised opting for a gradual, specialised hiring strategy to build a future-proof workforce. Now speaking on the 20VC podcast (via Fortune), Arora said that 90% of employees at large companies lack AI fluency, a gap he believes could determine career survival. “I think we’re back to a Darwinian moment where everybody has to figure out who’s really good,” he explained, stressing that workers must learn independently as no formal university courses exist to prepare them.The comments made by Arora come amid widespread layoffs tied to AI adoption. A 2025 Orgvue study found that 39% of employers have already made redundancies due to AI, while companies like Coinbase, Block, and Cloudflare have slashed thousands of jobs. Arora contrasted his approach with CEOs such as Brian Armstrong and Jack Dorsey, who cut 30–40% of staff, saying: “They’ve figured out there’s no redemption. ‘I can’t train these people, I’m going to just find the people who are going to come in and help me do this stuff. ’”At Palo Alto Networks, Arora is letting natural attrition—about 2% of employees leaving each month—reshape the workforce. He replaces departing staff with AI-fluent talent recruited through hackathons, aiming to transform 20–25% of his team within a year and achieve majority AI literacy in three years.
Article Summary: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora says AI token efficiency must drop to 20% within the next 12 months and as much as 90% by the following year. Arora said that 90% of employees at large companies lack AI fluency, a gap that could determine career survival.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Michael Dell: I can predict things, I can improve the uptime and the reliability, I can intervene and cause a better outcome before there's a problem
Article Text:
What Michael Dell meant

Why Michael Dell’s quote still matters

Dell Technologies founder and CEO Michael Dell said in a 2017 interview with Forbes that companies can use growing amounts of data and emerging technologies to predict problems before they happen. Speaking about how businesses can make better use of data, Dell said, "I can predict things. I can improve the uptime and the reliability. I can intervene and cause a better outcome before there's a problem." He explained that organisations were only beginning to unlock the value of their data and pointed to what he called "narrow artificial intelligence" as one of the technologies making this possible.During the interview, Dell said businesses were creating and storing more data than ever before. He described data as the "fuel" behind advances in artificial intelligence and machine intelligence. According to him, companies were only using a small portion of the information they collected, even though that data could help improve products, services and decision-making.Dell explained that as organisations gather more historical and real-time data, they can begin to identify patterns that were previously difficult to spot.This allows businesses to predict equipment failures, improve system reliability and take action before customers are affected.When Dell spoke about improving "uptime and reliability," he was referring to keeping business systems, networks and digital services running smoothly with fewer interruptions. Instead of reacting after a problem occurs, companies can use data-driven tools to detect early warning signs and prevent disruptions.Although Michael Dell made these remarks in 2017, the idea has become increasingly relevant as businesses adopt more data-driven technologies.Today, organisations across industries use predictive systems to monitor equipment, improve cybersecurity, manage cloud infrastructure and optimise operations. These tools analyse large amounts of data to identify risks and recommend actions before problems become serious.Dell also said that many companies were only beginning to understand how valuable their data could become over time. As more connected devices generate information, he believed the ability to use that data effectively would become a key advantage for businesses.
Article Summary: Dell Technologies founder and CEO Michael Dell said in a 2017 interview with Forbes that companies can use growing amounts of data and emerging technologies to predict problems before they happen. Dell said businesses were creating and storing more data than ever before. He described data as the "fuel" behind advances in artificial intelligence and machine intelligence.

Article Title: Months after Uber COO said that the company burnt its full AI budget for 2026 in less than four months, CTO Praveen Naga shares update on Agentic AI: Today, 99% of our engineers…
Article Text:
Uber CTO says company is moving beyond ‘Tokenmaxxing’



Read what Uber CTO Praveen Naga said



Agentic AI

adoption is on fire at @Uber, and it's changing the way we build, not just in engineering, but across the entire company.

Today, 99% of our engineers use AI tools. More than 70% of pull requests are attributed to local or cloud agents. And our engineers have built 2,500+ agent skills across the software development lifecycle.

Those numbers are exciting, but they led us to a much bigger question:

How do we bring agentic AI beyond engineering?

Finance. Legal. Operations. Marketing. Customer Support. HR. Procurement.

These functions run on complex workflows that are often manual, highly nuanced, and spread across dozens of systems. You can't automate them effectively by looking at process diagrams or documentation. You have to understand how the work actually gets done.

So we created something called Agentic Pods.

The idea is simple.

We handpicked ~30 of our most AI-proficient engineers (people with deep knowledge of Uber's systems) and paired each of them with a domain expert from a business function.

Then we gave every pod just two weeks.

• Days 1 – 2: Shadow the expert. Observe every step. Document workflows. Ask questions. Build intuition.

• Day 3: Prioritize opportunities based on scale, repetition, business impact, and data availability.

• Days 4 – 5: Build a working agent alongside the person doing the job.

• Days 6 – 9: Validate with several others performing the same work. Does it generalize? Does it actually make their job better?

• Day 10: Ship.

In just the past two months, we've run 16 Agentic Pods across 16 different business functions.

• Capital allocation across 150 cities: 15 hours → 30 minutes.

• Financial pacing reports: 2 days → 10 minutes.

• Marketing web quality assurance: 2 weeks → 50 minutes.

• Support workflow creation: 9,000 manual workflows → self-service automation.

The productivity gains are impressive, but what surprised us most wasn't the speed.

• It was how quickly engineers embedded in unfamiliar domains uncovered opportunities that had been hiding in plain sight.

• The biggest wins rarely come from automating one task. They come from rethinking an entire workflow. Once you redesign the workflow around AI, you often eliminate handoffs, remove unnecessary approvals, replace legacy tooling, reduce vendor spend, and dramatically accelerate decision-making.

• The workflow becomes the unit of automation - not the individual task.

• The most impactful agent skills cut across teams, orgs, functions, tools, and systems.

The biggest lesson? The best AI opportunities are rarely visible from the outside.

You discover them by sitting next to the people doing the work, understanding every friction point, and building with them, not for them.

We're now forming a dedicated team to scale this further and go deeper. They'll deeply understand the work, redesign it from the ground up, and use AI to fundamentally change how the business operates.

It's exciting times!

Uber’s push into artificial intelligence (AI) has been a rollercoaster ride. Earlier this year, the ride-hailing giant faced issue over its AI spending, with COO Andrew Macdonald noting the difficulty in justifying the company's “tokenmaxxing”, which is essentially the high cost of large-scale AI usage. Moreover, CTO Praveen Naga previously revealed that the company had burned through its entire planned budget for Claude Code in less than four months. However, Naga has provided an update, saying Uber has shifted its strategy from simply consuming AI services to systematically embedding “Agentic AI” into the core of its business, achieving a level of adoption where 99% of its engineers now use AI tools.To bridge the gap between high AI costs and real-world efficiency, Uber launched a project called “Agentic Pods”. The goal was to stop treating AI as an expensive experiment and start using it to redesign complex, manual workflows across departments like Finance, Legal and Marketing.Naga said that the company handpicked approximately 30 of its most AI-proficient engineers and paired them directly with domain experts – the employees who actually perform the work. The teams operated on a strict, two-week schedule. The claimed that in just two months, Uber successfully ran 16 of these “Agentic Pods” across 16 different business functions, and noted that the efficiency gains were significant.
Article Summary: Uber CTO Praveen Naga says company is moving beyond ‘Tokenmaxxing’ Naga: “Agentic AI is on fire at @Uber, and it's changing the way we build, not just in engineering, but across the entire company"

Article Title: Dell's Indrajit Belgundi on how the company is rewriting what a workstation is for its Indian customers
Article Text:
Indrajit Belgundi, Senior Director and General Manager, Client Solutions Group, Dell Technologies India

"We all hear about the token costs coming down," Indrajit Belgundi says, and then he turns the sentence around. "But the number of tokens being used is increasing exponentially." It is the kind of observation that sounds like a footnote and is actually a thesis. Belgundi, Senior Director and General Manager, Client Solutions Group, Dell Technologies India, is describing, in passing, why the workstation, a machine most professionals had mentally retired to the world of render farms and CAD jockeys, is being handed a second life, and why he thinks India's professionals are the ones who will give it that life.For most of a decade the workstation had a settled identity. It was the powerful, slightly unglamorous box that architects, engineers and visual-effects houses bought because their software demanded it and nobody else's did. The rest of the office moved to thin laptops and, eventually, to the cloud. Compute became something you rented by the hour from a data centre you would never see, and for most workloads that was the smarter deal: someone else owned the hardware, absorbed the depreciation and handled the upgrades. That arrangement held right up until AI started sending the bill, and Belgundi's arithmetic is the reason it broke.The shift is in the shape of the work. Traditional AI was one prompt, one response, a question in, an answer out, a predictable unit of cost.Agentic AI is a different animal: multiple specialised agents collaborate, iterate and spawn fresh tasks on their own, each reading and writing at length to resolve what began as a single request.Token consumption compounds rather than adds. Unit prices fall while total usage climbs faster, so the meter keeps rising even as each tick gets cheaper, and because the agents run themselves, the bill is no longer something you can forecast neatly at the start of a quarter. At which point the old buy-or-rent question reopens on new terms. Dell 's answer is to put the compute back on the desk. It has built the Dell Pro Precision portfolio and, sitting on top of it, a Deskside Agentic AI solution designed to make that case concrete. The reasoning rests on where AI's actual work happens: more than half of agentic workflows, Dell says, run on open-weight models in the 30-to-284-billion parameter range, the workmanlike middle tier that does the bulk reasoning while trillion-parameter models take the headlines. That tier fits on local hardware.Run it there instead of in the cloud, Dell claims, and an organisation can cut spend by up to 87% over two years, a figure worth reading as Dell's own projection, offered alongside an IDC brief the company commissioned with Intel. The strategy it points to is tiered rather than absolute: run the workhorse models locally, reserve cloud calls only for the largest frontier systems, and stop paying metered API fees for the routine reasoning that makes up most of the workload.The hardware to run it spans a deliberate range. At the compact end sits the Dell Pro Max with GB10, sized for 30-to-200-billion parameter models and pitched at individual developers and analysts prototyping a single agent. At the other end is the Dell Pro Max with GB300, built around NVIDIA's Grace Blackwell Ultra superchip to run inference on frontier-scale models from 120 billion up to a trillion parameters. Between and beneath them are the Pro Precision towers and mobile workstations that most professionals will actually buy. What ties the family together is NVIDIA's NemoClaw reference stack, CrowdStrike security and Dell's own services wrapped around the deployment: the difference, Dell would argue, between handing a team raw silicon and handing them something that works out of the box.That distinction is easier to grasp through the uses Dell has mapped out. A deskside code assistant runs multiple coding agents locally to write, review and test software, keeping intellectual property inside the building and the token bill at zero. A research assistant analyses large document collections without uploading sensitive or pre-publication material to anyone's cloud. And a private assistant offers a fully isolated environment for regulated industries, one built to satisfy HIPAA, GDPR and ITAR, the kind of alphabet soup that turns a data-sovereignty preference into a legal requirement.Which is where the workstation stops being a faster PC and becomes something closer to a private AI lab, one where the proprietary data never leaves the room. For an Indian bank or hospital weighing the same decision, that containment is often the argument that matters more than the cost curve.Belgundi is careful not to sort this by vertical. Dell names software engineering, higher education and research, healthcare and life sciences, and the legal-financial-defence cluster as its audiences, but he prefers to start from the workload and fit the machine to it rather than lead with an industry. What he is willing to be pinned to is the local target, and it isn't the enterprises that already own workstations. It's the small and mid-size businesses that never did, the fragmented middle of the Indian market that long balked at enterprise prices for enterprise reliability.Dell arrives with survey numbers to argue the hesitation is ending: among the Indian organisations it polled, 95% reported higher productivity from workstation users, 77% cited strong use for AI deployment, and 76% expect these machines to claim a larger share of their fleet within five years. Belgundi's term for what those buyers want is "future-proofing": hardware built not for this year's software but for the applications nobody has written yet, good for the next two to five years.The devices themselves carry the fingerprints of that feedback. Indian customers wanted power without the bulk, so the Pro Precision 5 series 14S arrives at 1. 4kg, the thinnest workstation Dell has built, running Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or AMD Ryzen AI 400 silicon with edge inferencing from its integrated graphics. They wanted stamina without compromise, so the Pro Precision 7 series folds a 50 TOPS NPU and up to NVIDIA RTX Pro 3000 Blackwell graphics into a chassis rated for 19 hours. Prices open at Rs 1,49,000 for the 5 series, Rs 2,25,000 for the 7 series and Rs 89,000 for the 7 T1, with the GB10 deskside system at Rs 4,99,000; the 5 series 14S and 16S reach buyers on August 10.For a decade the workstation lost every argument to the cloud, because renting compute was cheaper than owning it. AI has quietly reversed the sum. The box under the desk isn't a nostalgia play or a niche for engineers anymore: it's a bet that the cheapest place to run tomorrow's AI is the one you already paid for. India's professionals will settle whether Dell has read the arithmetic right.
Article Summary: Dell has built the Dell Pro Precision portfolio and, sitting on top of it, a Deskside Agentic AI solution. The aim is to put the compute back on the desk. More than half of agentic workflows run on open-weight models in the 30-to-284-billion range.
